title: The best vulnerability-finding model missed 160 of 231 known bugs at 96.3% precision
summary: Vercel's DeepsecBench scores 25 model configurations on finding real vulnerabilities in a real codebase, and the leader reports 71 of the 231 known findings.
takeaways: Treat an agent's security scan as a queue of findings to triage and grade it on what it missed — the best configuration on DeepsecBench reported 71 of 231 known vulnerabilities.
The leader printed only three false positives, so at the top of the board the risk has moved from noise you can see to the 69% you never hear about.
The benchmark's method is the transferable part: recall against a human-judged golden set, weighted twice as heavily as precision, with the median of three runs published.

body:
## What happened

On 27 July, Malte Ubl and Eric Dodds released [DeepsecBench](https://vercel.com/blog/deepsecbench-evaluating-model-performance-in-finding-cybersecurity-vulnerabilities), a benchmark for how well models find security vulnerabilities in application code. It runs on an open-source codebase pinned ["at a commit state just before a large number of vulnerabilities were fixed"](https://vercel.com/blog/deepsecbench-evaluating-model-performance-in-finding-cybersecurity-vulnerabilities) — 50 entry-point files and "a golden set of 231 human-judged findings." The top configuration, GPT-5.6 Sol at xhigh, [reports 71 of 231: 30.7% recall at 96.3% precision, three false positives, $55.98 and 3h 39m](https://vercel.com/ai-gateway/leaderboards/deepsecbench). Claude Opus 5 at max is second with 65 of 231 at $127.93, and nothing on the 25-row board clears 31% recall.

## Why it matters

What the leading configurations print is now mostly real; the risk sits in the seven bugs in ten that are never mentioned. Silence from a scanner that is usually right reads like a clean bill of health, and nothing in the output separates "this file is fine" from "I never got there."

## How it works

1. **Grade against a human golden set.** A fixed denominator of 231 human-judged findings, which the model cannot shrink by staying quiet.
2. **Weight recall over precision.** Score = 100 × 5PR/(4P+R), ["weighting recall (R) twice as much as precision (P), because missed vulnerabilities will go unfixed, while false positives don't make your codebase less secure."](https://vercel.com/blog/deepsecbench-evaluating-model-performance-in-finding-cybersecurity-vulnerabilities)
3. **Run it more than once.** The published number is ["the median of the three runs."](https://vercel.com/blog/deepsecbench-evaluating-model-performance-in-finding-cybersecurity-vulnerabilities)

> A finding you can trust tells you nothing about the file the scan never mentioned.

## The catch

It is a vendor benchmark, ["based on the deepsec cyber harness"](https://vercel.com/ai-gateway/leaderboards/deepsecbench) Vercel builds, and its construction is secret, so nobody outside can reproduce it: ["We don't disclose the repository, the commit, the files, or the findings, so there is nothing for models to train against."](https://vercel.com/blog/deepsecbench-evaluating-model-performance-in-finding-cybersecurity-vulnerabilities) The board is incomplete too: ["Anthropic's most capable model, Fable 5, is absent because it declines security work, including defensive tasks."](https://vercel.com/blog/deepsecbench-evaluating-model-performance-in-finding-cybersecurity-vulnerabilities) The hits need care as well — a 15 July study on a Python repository benchmark found [26-55% of true positives "are correct predictions supported by flawed rationales"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13439), and the 20 July [RECEIPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18575) work on agentic XSS discovery replays every candidate deterministically because "a coding agent's claims cannot be trusted on their own."
